A **finite row-stochastic kernel** is a finite set $X$ and a matrix $P=(P_{xy})_{x,y\in X}$ with $P_{xy}\in[0,1]$ and

$$\sum_{y\in X}P_{xy}=1\qquad(x\in X).$$

The row convention is $P_{xy}=\Pr(Y=y\mid X=x)$: distributions are row vectors and one transition sends $\mu$ to $\mu P$. If $X=\varnothing$, the row conditions are vacuous and there is no probability distribution on $X$. No stationary distribution, reversibility, irreducibility, aperiodicity, or efficient circuit access is part of this definition.

Let $(X,P,\pi)$ be a finite reversible Markov chain with positive stationary law, as in [[def-qa-17-finite-reversible-chain]], and let $\mathcal M\subseteq X$ be a set of marked states. Its **stationary marked mass** is

$$\varepsilon:=\pi(\mathcal M)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal M}\pi_x.$$

For a specified threshold $\varepsilon_0\in(0,1]$, the **marked-set detection promise problem** has yes-instances with $\mathcal M\ne\varnothing$ and $\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon_0$, and no-instances with $\mathcal M=\varnothing$. The required classical output is one bit distinguishing these two cases; its permitted failure probability is a separate algorithm input. In the uniform-chain case, $\pi_x=1/|X|$, so $\varepsilon=|\mathcal M|/|X|$.

The **marked-state finding promise problem** has inputs with $\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon_0$ and requires a classical output $x\in\mathcal M$. It is a different output relation from detection. A claimed output is checked by the declared finite projective measurement and marked predicate; the corresponding outcome law is [[def-qc-projective-measurement]] and [[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]]. The encoding of $X$, the coherent marked predicate, and all state-preparation and transition circuits are supplied input data, not consequences of the finite chain matrix.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: For any vector $z\in\mathbb C^X$, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz, obtained by applying [F6] to $(\sqrt{Q_{xy}})_y$ and $(\sqrt{Q_{xy}}z_y)_y$, gives $|(Qz)_x|^2\le\sum_y Q_{xy}|z_y|^2$. Summing over $x$ and using symmetry, so that every column sum is also $1$, yields $\|Qz\|^2\le\|z\|^2$. Since $Q$ is self-adjoint by its real symmetric matrix and [F4], [F3] gives a real orthonormal eigenbasis; the contraction inequality forces every eigenvalue of $Q$ into $[-1,1]$. Thus $P=(I+Q)/2$ is self-adjoint with spectrum in $[0,1]$. Its row sums are $1$, so $P\mathbf u=\mathbf u$.

If $U=\varnothing$, then $P_U=0$ and the conclusion follows from [F5]. Otherwise choose a unit vector $z$ supported on $U$ and write $z=\alpha\mathbf u+v$ with $v\perp\mathbf u$. [F6] applied to $\langle z,\mathbf u\rangle=\langle z,\Pi_U\mathbf u\rangle$ gives $|\alpha|^2\le\|\Pi_U\mathbf u\|^2=|U|/n=1-\varepsilon$, so $\|v\|^2=1-|\alpha|^2$.

The orthogonal complement $\mathbf u^\perp$ is invariant under $P$ by self-adjointness and $P\mathbf u=\mathbf u$. Its eigenvalues are at most $1-\delta$ by the stated second-eigenvalue hypothesis. Therefore $\langle z,Pz\rangle=|\alpha|^2+\langle v,Pv\rangle\le |\alpha|^2+(1-\delta)\|v\|^2\le1-\delta\varepsilon$.

The compression $P_U$ is positive semidefinite because $\langle z,P_Uz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle\ge0$ for every vector supported on $U$, by the nonnegative spectrum in step 1.1. It is self-adjoint, so its operator norm is its largest eigenvalue; equivalently it is the maximum of its unit-vector Rayleigh quotients. Step 2.1 bounds each such quotient by $1-\delta\varepsilon$, proving the result.

Let $X$ be the finite state set, $P$ its row-transition matrix, $\mathcal M\subseteq X$ the marked set, $U=X\setminus\mathcal M$, and $P_{UU}$ the principal submatrix indexed by $U$. For an initial probability row vector $\mu$, the **hitting-time survival law** is

$$\Pr_\mu(\tau_{\mathcal M}>t):=\mu_U P_{UU}^{\,t}\mathbf 1_U,\qquad t\in\mathbb N_0,$$

where $\mu_U$ is the restriction of $\mu$ to $U$ and $\mathbf 1_U$ is the all-ones column vector on $U$. This is the finite sum of probabilities of all length-$t$ paths that remain in $U$; it does not require a path-space construction. For $U=\varnothing$ the right side is $0$; for $\mathcal M=\varnothing$ it is $1$.

The hitting time $\tau_{\mathcal M}:=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t\in\mathcal M\}$ is the $\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$-valued variable determined by this survival law. Its extended expectation is $\mathbb E_\mu\tau_{\mathcal M}=\sum_{t\ge0}\Pr_\mu(\tau_{\mathcal M}>t)$, and a constant-success hitting bound is a specified integer $t$ for which $\Pr_\mu(\tau_{\mathcal M}\le t)$ is bounded below by a positive constant. These resource conventions are kept separate.

derivations.claim: Let $u_U=|U|^{-1/2}\mathbf1_U$. For the uniform initial law on $U$, [F2] gives $\Pr(\tau_{\mathcal M}>t)=\langle u_U,P_{UU}^{\,t}u_U\rangle$. Since $P_{UU}$ is positive semidefinite, it has eigenvalues in $[0,1-\delta\varepsilon]$ by [F1]; its $t$th power therefore has operator norm at most $(1-\delta\varepsilon)^t$. [F3] and $\|u_U\|=1$ prove the survival bound, including $t=0$.

Put $a=\delta\varepsilon$. For $0<a<1$, the nonnegative-integer tail formula in [F2] and the finite geometric partial sums give $\mathbb E\tau_{\mathcal M}=\sum_{t\ge0}\Pr(\tau_{\mathcal M}>t)\le\sum_{t\ge0}(1-a)^t=1/a$. For the constant-success bound choose $t=\lceil1/a\rceil$. Since $(1-a)(1+a)=1-a^2\le1$, we have $1-a\le(1+a)^{-1}$; the finite binomial expansion gives $(1+a)^t\ge1+ta\ge2$. Hence $(1-a)^t\le(1+a)^{-t}\le1/2$. If $a=1$, step 1.1 gives zero no-hit probability for every $t\ge1$, so one step suffices. The case $\mathcal M=X$ is immediate from the definition.

$$T|x\rangle=|x\rangle\otimes\sum_{y\in X}\sqrt{P_{xy}}|y\rangle,\qquad S|x,y\rangle=|y,x\rangle.$$

Every scalar square root is the unique nonnegative real root. Define the **discriminant** by $D:=T^*ST$, using the adjoint characterized by $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,T^*w\rangle$ for the root inner product, which is linear in its first argument. The row-preparation map is an isometry; its complete verification is [[thm-qa-17-discriminant-self-adjoint]]. This is the general row-stochastic construction and assumes no reversibility.

For every finite row-stochastic kernel, the map $T$ of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]] satisfies $T^*T=I$ and is an isometry, and the matrix entries of $D=T^*ST$ are

$$D_{xy}=\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}.$$

Hence $D$ is real symmetric, self-adjoint, and $\|D\|\le1$. If $(X,P,\pi)$ is also finite reversible, then

$$D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt\pi)\,P\,\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt\pi).$$

Every eigenvalue of $D$ is real and belongs to $[-1,1]$. The empty state set has the zero endomorphism and empty spectrum; the similarity assertion is only made when a positive stationary probability vector is supplied.

Let $P$ be a finite symmetric row-stochastic matrix on $X$, and let $\mathcal M\subseteq X$, $U=X\setminus\mathcal M$. Define the row-stochastic absorbing matrix

$$P'_{xy}=\begin{cases}1,&x=y\in\mathcal M,\\0,&x\in\mathcal M,\ y\ne x,\\P_{xy},&x\in U.\end{cases}$$

For the general row-stochastic discriminant $D(P')_{xy}=\sqrt{P'_{xy}P'_{yx}}$ of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]],

$$D(P')=P_{UU}\oplus I_{\mathcal M},$$

where $P_{UU}$ is the principal submatrix on $U$. In general $P'$ need not be symmetric or reversible.

Let $D=T^*ST$ be the discriminant of a finite row-stochastic kernel and let $U=S(2TT^*-I)$ and $W=U^2$. For every eigenvalue $\lambda\in(-1,1)$ of $D$, counted with multiplicity, its invariant planes contribute eigenvalues

$$\exp(i\arccos\lambda),\ \exp(-i\arccos\lambda)\quad\text{for }U,\qquad \exp(2i\arccos\lambda),\ \exp(-2i\arccos\lambda)\quad\text{for }W.$$

For each eigendirection with $\lambda=1$ (respectively $\lambda=-1$), the plane collapses to a line on which $U$ acts as $+I$ (respectively $-I$), so $W$ acts as $+I$. On the remaining subspace $K=(\operatorname{ran}T+\operatorname{ran}(ST))^\perp$, $U=-S$ and its eigenvalues lie in $\{+1,-1\}$; therefore all eigenvalues of $W$ there are $+1$. If $X=\varnothing$, both spaces are zero and the statements about eigenvalues are vacuous.

Let $U$ be a unitary on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$. Let $\Theta\subset[0,1)$ be its finite set of distinct eigenphases, and let $\Pi_\theta$ denote the orthogonal projection onto the full eigenspace for eigenvalue $\exp(2\pi i\theta)$; degeneracies are grouped in one projection. For $Q=2^m$, $m\ge1$, define
$$a_y(\theta):=Q^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{Q-1}\exp(2\pi ij(\theta-y/Q)),\qquad K_y:=\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}a_y(\theta)\Pi_\theta.$$
For a unit input $\psi=\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}\Pi_\theta\psi$, the unnormalized branch vector is $K_y\psi$ and
$$p_y=\|K_y\psi\|^2=\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}|a_y(\theta)|^2\|\Pi_\theta\psi\|^2.$$
If $p_y>0$, the conditional vector is $K_y\psi/\sqrt{p_y}$; if $p_y=0$, no conditional vector is assigned. The outcome law is an eigenspace-weighted mixture, while the conditional branch can retain coherent cross terms between distinct eigenspaces.

After discarding the phase register, the induced system instrument has branch maps $\mathcal I_y(X)=K_yXK_y^\dagger$ for operators $X$ on $H$. More generally, for a density operator $\rho$ on $H\otimes R$, where $R$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional reference space, the unnormalized reference-preserving branch after measuring and discarding the phase register is
$$\mathcal I_y^{(R)}(\rho)=(K_y\otimes I_R)\rho(K_y^\dagger\otimes I_R).$$
Its probability is $\operatorname{tr}\mathcal I_y^{(R)}(\rho)$, and the conditional state is $\mathcal I_y^{(R)}(\rho)/\operatorname{tr}\mathcal I_y^{(R)}(\rho)$ exactly when that probability is positive. With $w_\theta=\operatorname{tr}((\Pi_\theta\otimes I_R)\rho)$, the reference outcome law is $p_y=\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}|a_y(\theta)|^2w_\theta$, where $w_\theta\ge0$ and $\sum_\theta w_\theta=1$. If every eigenphase is on the $Q$-grid, then $K_y=\Pi_{y/Q}$ when $y/Q\in\Theta$ and $K_y=0$ otherwise, so the instrument branch is $X\mapsto K_yXK_y^\dagger$. If any eigenphase is off-grid, its nonzero coefficient has modulus less than one in every $K_y$, so $K_y^\dagger K_y$ is not a projection and the induced instrument is not the spectral projection instrument.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Hence $D$ is real symmetric, self-adjoint, and $\|D\|\le1$. If $(X,P,\pi)$ is also finite reversible, then

Every eigenvalue of $D$ is real and belongs to $[-1,1]$. The empty state set has the zero endomorphism and empty spectrum; the similarity assertion is only made when a positive stationary probability vector is supplied.

For a real $x\in[-1,1]$, define its circular distance to the nearest integer by
$$d_{\mathbb T}(x):=\min\{|x|,\,1-|x|\}.$$
Here $|x|$ is the real absolute value and $\min$ is the minimum of the displayed finite set ([[def-real-order]], [[def-max-min]]); existence of this finite minimum follows from [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]. Both entries lie in $[0,1]$, so the value lies in $[0,1/2]$. If $|x|\le1/2$, the nearest integer is $0$; if $x>1/2$, it is $1$; if $x<-1/2$, it is $-1$, so the formula is the distance to the nearest integer. For phases $\theta,\phi\in[0,1)$, their circular distance is $d_{\mathbb T}(\theta-\phi)$; the difference belongs to $(-1,1)$, the stated domain.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

derivations.claim: If $|X|=1$, the supplied predicate is evaluated on the sole label and the procedure returns the exact answer. Assume henceforth $|X|\ge2$. In the empty case $U=X$, $P'=P$, and the prepared row state is $T'|s\rangle$, where $|s\rangle=|X|^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in X}|x\rangle$. Symmetry of $P$ gives $T'|s\rangle=ST'|s\rangle$, so [F3] places it on the $+1$ eigenline and its phase is exactly zero. The first marked check cannot accept, and [F6] makes QPE output $y=0$, for which the strict cutoff fails. Thus neither branch falsely accepts.

In a nonempty instance write $\varepsilon=|\mathcal M|/|X|$. The first-register check measures a uniformly distributed label; if it is marked, the algorithm accepts immediately, including the endpoint $\mathcal M=X$. Otherwise $U=X\setminus\mathcal M$ is nonempty and the conditional row state is $T'|s_U\rangle$, with $|s_U\rangle=|U|^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in U}|x\rangle$. By [F10], each first-register outcome has squared norm $1/|X|$ under $T'$, and [F12] projects onto the sum of exactly the $|U|$ unmarked row vectors and normalizes it.

On $U$, [F1] and the promises give $0\le\lambda(P_{UU})\le1-\underline\delta\,\underline\varepsilon$. Hence its eigenvalues are at most $1-\underline\delta\,\underline\varepsilon<1$ and their one-reflection phases have circular distance from zero at least $\gamma_0/(2\pi)$. The state $T'|s_U\rangle$ lies in $\operatorname{ran}T'$ and is orthogonal to every marked row vector $T'|x\rangle$, $x\in\mathcal M$, because those vectors have a distinct first-register label; the orthogonality also follows from the isometry [F10]. It therefore has no marked $\lambda=1$ component and no component in $(\operatorname{ran}T'+\operatorname{ran}(ST'))^\perp$. The decomposition [F2] and spectral mapping [F3] show that all its spectral components are the nonzero-phase signal components just bounded.

The choice of $m$ gives $1-\underline\delta\,\underline\varepsilon\le\cos(\pi2^{5-m})$. By [F13], $\cos\gamma_0=1-\underline\delta\,\underline\varepsilon$, and [F14] with $\gamma_0\in[0,\pi]$ and $\pi2^{5-m}\in[0,\pi]$ therefore gives $\gamma_0\ge\pi2^{5-m}$, or $Q\ge32\pi/\gamma_0$. Thus the branch comparison in algorithm step 5 is exact: $d(y)>1/8$ implies $d(y)>\gamma_0/(4\pi)$, while for $d(y)\le1/8$ both angles lie in $[0,\pi/2]$ and strict decrease of cosine makes $d(y)>\gamma_0/(4\pi)$ equivalent to $\cos(4\pi d(y))<1-\underline\delta\,\underline\varepsilon$; equality takes the rejected branch. To justify the needed distance comparison from the definition [F11], take $u=\theta-y/Q\in(-1,1)$ and $v=y/Q\in[0,1)$. Since $\theta=u+v\in[0,1)$, its distance to the nearest integer is at most its distance to the particular integer $a+b$; hence $$d_{\mathbb T}(\theta)\le|\theta-(a+b)|=|(u-a)+(v-b)|\le d_{\mathbb T}(u)+d_{\mathbb T}(v).$$ Thus $d(y):=d_{\mathbb T}(y/Q)\ge d_{\mathbb T}(\theta)-d_{\mathbb T}(\theta-y/Q)$. Let $(X,P,\pi)$ be a finite reversible Markov chain with positive stationary law, as in [[def-qa-17-finite-reversible-chain]], and let $\mathcal M\subseteq X$ be a set of marked states. Its **stationary marked mass** is

$$\varepsilon:=\pi(\mathcal M)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal M}\pi_x.$$

For a specified threshold $\varepsilon_0\in(0,1]$, the **marked-set detection promise problem** has yes-instances with $\mathcal M\ne\varnothing$ and $\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon_0$, and no-instances with $\mathcal M=\varnothing$. The required classical output is one bit distinguishing these two cases; its permitted failure probability is a separate algorithm input. In the uniform-chain case, $\pi_x=1/|X|$, so $\varepsilon=|\mathcal M|/|X|$.

The **marked-state finding promise problem** has inputs with $\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon_0$ and requires a classical output $x\in\mathcal M$. It is a different output relation from detection. A claimed output is checked by the declared finite projective measurement and marked predicate; the corresponding outcome law is [[def-qc-projective-measurement]] and [[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]]. The encoding of $X$, the coherent marked predicate, and all state-preparation and transition circuits are supplied input data, not consequences of the finite chain matrix.

For a finite reversible chain $(X,P,\pi)$, let $H_0=\{f:\sum_x\pi_xf_x=0\}$ with the weighted inner product from [[lem-qa-17-reversible-transition-self-adjoint-on-l2-pi]]. Define its **absolute spectral gap** by

$$\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P):=1-\|P|_{H_0}\|_{2,\pi}.$$

The norm of the restriction to the zero subspace is $0$ by [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]], so a one-state chain has absolute gap $1$. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is built into this definition: a reducible chain with a nonconstant stationary vector in $H_0$ can have gap $0$, and a periodic chain can have gap $0$ because of an eigenvalue $-1$. The eigenvalue form of the definition is proved in [[thm-qa-17-absolute-gap-eigenvalue-characterization]].

Let $(X,P,\pi)$ be a finite reversible chain and let $H_0=\{f:\sum_x\pi_xf_x=0\}$. If $H_0=\{0\}$, then $\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P)=1$. Otherwise,

$$\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P)=1-\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\sigma(P|_{H_0})\},$$

and $0\le\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P)\le1$. If there is a fixed function $f\notin\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}$, then its nonzero mean-zero component is fixed by $P$, so the gap is $0$.

Let $D=T^*ST$ be the discriminant of a finite row-stochastic kernel and let $U=S(2TT^*-I)$ and $W=U^2$. For every eigenvalue $\lambda\in(-1,1)$ of $D$, counted with multiplicity, its invariant planes contribute eigenvalues

$$\exp(i\arccos\lambda),\ \exp(-i\arccos\lambda)\quad\text{for }U,\qquad \exp(2i\arccos\lambda),\ \exp(-2i\arccos\lambda)\quad\text{for }W.$$

For each eigendirection with $\lambda=1$ (respectively $\lambda=-1$), the plane collapses to a line on which $U$ acts as $+I$ (respectively $-I$), so $W$ acts as $+I$. On the remaining subspace $K=(\operatorname{ran}T+\operatorname{ran}(ST))^\perp$, $U=-S$ and its eigenvalues lie in $\{+1,-1\}$; therefore all eigenvalues of $W$ there are $+1$. If $X=\varnothing$, both spaces are zero and the statements about eigenvalues are vacuous.

**Input.** An integer $m\ge1$; an $m$-qubit phase register; a finite-dimensional system register $H$; a unitary $U:H\to H$; a unit eigenvector $\psi$ with promised phase $\theta\in[0,1)$; and one of the forward access capabilities in [[def-qa-eigenphase-estimation-model]].

**Output.** A classical label $y\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}$ and its phase estimate $y/Q$, where $Q=2^m$.

**Instructions.**

1. Initialize the phase register in $|0^m\rangle$ and the system register in $\psi$.
2. Apply the Hadamard $H=(X+Z)/\sqrt2$ of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] to each phase wire. This prepares $Q^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{Q-1}|x\rangle\otimes\psi$ in the declared big-endian order.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,m-1$, apply the supplied controlled $U^{2^j}$ to control wire $q_{m-1-j}$ and the system. Under single controlled-unitary access, implement that operation with $2^j$ sequential calls to $C(U)$, as specified by the access model.
4. Apply the inverse of the positive-sign exact binary QFT circuit of [[def-qa-cyclic-quantum-fourier-transform]] and [[thm-qa-exact-binary-qft-circuit-correct]]. Construct it by reversing the chronological gate list and replacing each gate by its adjoint, including the final swaps and negating controlled-phase angles.
5. Perform the computational-basis projective measurement on the phase register. Its specified Lüders instrument has branch map $Z\mapsto (|y\rangle\langle y|\otimes I_H)Z(|y\rangle\langle y|\otimes I_H)$ for each label $y$ ([[def-qc-projective-measurement]], [[def-qc-instrument-and-conditional-state]]). Output the observed label $y$ and the ratio $y/Q$.

The inverse in step 4 is the inverse QFT, not $U^{-1}$; a forward QPE run makes no controlled inverse-unitary query. The coherent prefix is the circuit through step 4 before measurement. A consumer that coherently uncomputes this prefix needs the separate controlled inverse-power capability from [[def-qa-eigenphase-estimation-model]].

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $U:H\to H$ a unitary, and $\psi\in H$ a unit vector with a promised phase $\theta\in[0,1)$ such that
$$U\psi=\exp(2\pi i\theta)\psi.$$
For an integer $m\ge1$, let $Q=2^m$. The phase register is $(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m}$ with ordered computational basis indexed big-endian by
$x=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}b_k2^{m-1-k}$, where $b_k\in\{0,1\}$ ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]], [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]).
Thus the wire of weight $2^j$ is $q_{m-1-j}$.

There are distinct forward-access options:

1. **Controlled-power access.** The model explicitly supplies one controlled $U^{2^j}$ operation for each $j=0,\ldots,m-1$. Each use is counted as one controlled-power query; an implementation's ordinary gate cost is recorded separately.
2. **Single controlled-unitary access.** The model supplies calls to $C(U)=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,U)$ in the control-first order of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. A controlled $U^{2^j}$ may be implemented by $2^j$ sequential calls to $C(U)$; those calls are charged individually.

Optional **controlled inverse-power access** is a separate capability that explicitly supplies $C(U^{-2^j})$ for each required $j$. It is not implied by either forward option. It is needed only by a consuming procedure that reverses the controlled-power portion of a coherent QPE prefix. Reversing the inverse-QFT gate list does not use $U^{-1}$.

Finite ordered-register syntax is specified by [[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], gate action by [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]], and projective measurement outcomes by [[def-qc-projective-measurement]]. The definition is an access-model promise: it does not assert that the supplied controlled powers have an efficient construction or that $\theta$ has an exact $m$-bit expansion.

Let $m\ge1$, $Q=2^m$, and let the input be an eigenvector with
$U\psi=\exp(2\pi i\theta)\psi$, where $\theta\in[0,1)$.
For each $y\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}$, the probability of measuring $y$ in the algorithm of [[alg-qa-quantum-phase-estimation]] is
$$P_\theta(y)=Q^{-2}\left|\sum_{j=0}^{Q-1}\exp\!\left(2\pi i j(\theta-y/Q)\right)\right|^2.$$
Thus the finite outcome kernel is defined at every phase, including $Q\theta\in\mathbb Z$; no quotient with a zero denominator is needed in this formula.

For $n\in\mathbb N$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$S_n(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}z^j,$$
with the empty sum $S_0(z)=0$. Then
$$S_n(z)=\begin{cases}\iota_{\mathbb C}(n),&z=1,\\[2pt](1-z^n)/(1-z),&z\ne1,\end{cases}$$
where $\iota_{\mathbb C}$ is the canonical natural embedding of $\mathbb N$ into $\mathbb C$.

For $Q=2^m$, $\theta\in[0,1)$, and integer $y$, setting
$z=\exp(2\pi i(\theta-y/Q))$ gives
$z^Q=\exp(2\pi iQ\theta)$; moreover $z=1$ exactly when
$Q\theta-y\in Q\mathbb Z$.

For $0\le u\le1/2$ and $v\ge0$,
$$\sin(\pi u)\ge2u,\qquad \sin(v)\le v.$$
Let $m\ge1$, $Q=2^m$, and $\theta\in[0,1)$. If $Q\theta=t\in\mathbb Z$, then $t\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}$, phase estimation returns $y=t$ with probability $1$, and every other output has probability $0$.

Let $U$ be a unitary on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$. Let $\Theta\subset[0,1)$ be its finite set of distinct eigenphases, and let $\Pi_\theta$ denote the orthogonal projection onto the full eigenspace for eigenvalue $\exp(2\pi i\theta)$; degeneracies are grouped in one projection. For $Q=2^m$, $m\ge1$, define
$$a_y(\theta):=Q^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{Q-1}\exp(2\pi ij(\theta-y/Q)),\qquad K_y:=\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}a_y(\theta)\Pi_\theta.$$
For a unit input $\psi=\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}\Pi_\theta\psi$, the unnormalized branch vector is $K_y\psi$ and
$$p_y=\|K_y\psi\|^2=\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}|a_y(\theta)|^2\|\Pi_\theta\psi\|^2.$$
If $p_y>0$, the conditional vector is $K_y\psi/\sqrt{p_y}$; if $p_y=0$, no conditional vector is assigned. The outcome law is an eigenspace-weighted mixture, while the conditional branch can retain coherent cross terms between distinct eigenspaces.

After discarding the phase register, the induced system instrument has branch maps $\mathcal I_y(X)=K_yXK_y^\dagger$ for operators $X$ on $H$. More generally, for a density operator $\rho$ on $H\otimes R$, where $R$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional reference space, the unnormalized reference-preserving branch after measuring and discarding the phase register is
$$\mathcal I_y^{(R)}(\rho)=(K_y\otimes I_R)\rho(K_y^\dagger\otimes I_R).$$
Its probability is $\operatorname{tr}\mathcal I_y^{(R)}(\rho)$, and the conditional state is $\mathcal I_y^{(R)}(\rho)/\operatorname{tr}\mathcal I_y^{(R)}(\rho)$ exactly when that probability is positive. With $w_\theta=\operatorname{tr}((\Pi_\theta\otimes I_R)\rho)$, the reference outcome law is $p_y=\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}|a_y(\theta)|^2w_\theta$, where $w_\theta\ge0$ and $\sum_\theta w_\theta=1$. If every eigenphase is on the $Q$-grid, then $K_y=\Pi_{y/Q}$ when $y/Q\in\Theta$ and $K_y=0$ otherwise, so the instrument branch is $X\mapsto K_yXK_y^\dagger$. If any eigenphase is off-grid, its nonzero coefficient has modulus less than one in every $K_y$, so $K_y^\dagger K_y$ is not a projection and the induced instrument is not the spectral projection instrument.

Let $m\ge1$ and $Q=2^m$. Count costs in the ideal continuous-rotation submodel, where each exact controlled phase used by the binary QFT is one gate. If the controlled powers $C(U^{2^j})$, $0\le j<m$, are supplied as one query each, one run uses exactly $m$ controlled-power queries. If the only oracle is $C(U)$, the repeated implementation uses exactly $Q-1$ controlled-$U$ queries. If the supplied controlled-power circuits have ordinary gate counts $C_j$, the unitary gate count after the eigenstate input is provided is
$$\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}C_j+2m+\frac{m(m-1)}2+\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor.$$
The final register measurement reads $m$ bits and is not included in this unitary gate count. No cost-free power construction, fixed finite gate alphabet, uniform family, or state-preparation bound is asserted.

The series

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k}{2k+1}$$

converges, and its sum is $\pi/4$. More precisely, for every natural $N$,

$$\frac{\pi}{4}=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\frac{(-1)^k}{2k+1}+R_N,\qquad |R_N|\le\frac1{2N+3},$$

where

$$R_N:=(-1)^{N+1}\int_0^1\frac{x^{2N+2}}{1+x^2}\,dx.$$

When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For all real $u,v$,

$$|\sin u-\sin v|\le|u-v|,$$

and

$$|\cos u-\cos v|\le|u-v|.$$

Thus sine and cosine are Lipschitz functions on $\mathbb R$, each with
Lipschitz constant $1$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$, and let $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite projective measurement on $H$. Then $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$ lies in $[0,1]$ for every $a$, and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}p_\rho(a)=1$.

This is the finite-generation and execution procedure OP2 in `research/quantum-algorithms-planning/operational-contracts.md`, section “OP2 — MNRS approximate reflection and finite tolerant recursive finding”, transcribed with its declared constants and charged branches.

**Input.** A finite ergodic reversible row chain $(X,P,\pi)$ with $\pi_x>0$, a supplied positive dyadic rational lower absolute-gap bound $\delta_0$, a dyadic rational marked-mass lower bound $\varepsilon_0>0$ with promise $\pi(\mathcal M)=0$ or $\pi(\mathcal M)\ge\varepsilon_0$, a coherent marked-bit check of cost $C$, and a dyadic rational failure target $\rho\in(0,1)$. These finite parameter encodings suffice for real positive promises: choose dyadic lower bounds within a factor of two of the gap and nonzero marked-mass bounds, and a dyadic target in $(\rho_*/2,\rho_*]$ for desired failure probability $\rho_*$.  Write $|\sqrt\pi\rangle=\sum_{x\in X}\sqrt{\pi_x}|x\rangle$ and let $T|x\rangle=|x\rangle\sum_y\sqrt{P_{xy}}|y\rangle$ be the row isometry of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]]. The supplied clean preparation $A_\pi$ maps its specified blank input to the **stationary edge state**
$$|\pi_{\rm edge}\rangle=T|\sqrt\pi\rangle=\sum_{x\in X}\sqrt{\pi_x}|x\rangle\sum_{y\in X}\sqrt{P_{xy}}|y\rangle,$$
returns all its work registers to their specified blank states, and has charged cost $S$. The row-access interface of [[def-qa-17-walk-access-model]] supplies the row-preparation unitary $V_P$, its inverse, controlled forward and inverse calls, the clean-state reflection $R_0$ and its controlled call, and the swap $S$ and its controlled call. On the clean-work logical walk space these implement $R_A=2TT^*-I=V_PR_0V_P^*$, $U=SR_A$, and $W=U^2$, with each constituent charged. Supply controlled calls to $W$ and $W^*$ for the coherent QPE circuits and an exact controlled $R_A$ for the all-zero branch. A single bound $U_0$ covers each controlled $W$ or $W^*$ call and the controlled $R_A$ call, including their factorwise implementation costs. A matrix $P$ alone supplies none of these circuits.

**Marked check and retained-state instrument.** Write $m(x)=\mathbf1_{\mathcal M}(x)$. The supplied exact coherent check is a unitary $B_{\mathcal M}$ with separately supplied inverse and specified fresh flag $F$ and scratch $J$. On the declared logical encoding it satisfies, for every $x\in X$, $b\in\{0,1\}$, and vector $\eta$ of all existing remaining registers,
$$B_{\mathcal M}(|x\rangle|\eta\rangle|b\rangle_F|0\rangle_J)=|x\rangle|\eta\rangle|b\mathbin\oplus m(x)\rangle_F|0\rangle_J.$$
Its unitary extension outside the logical encoding is supplied too. Thus it preserves the first label and every existing walk, phase, data, and work auxiliary on clean new scratch. In the relevant query/check cost coordinates, $C$ bounds each forward and inverse check call; declare the flag-readout cost separately and include it in $C$ in any coordinate that counts readout as a check. A flag readout uses no value-oracle query. Gate, output-bit, and new flag/scratch costs are separately priced.

On the whole existing register space set $\Pi_1=\Pi_{\mathcal M}=(\sum_{x\in\mathcal M}|x\rangle\langle x|)\otimes I_{\rm rest}$ and $\Pi_0=I-\Pi_{\mathcal M}$, with identity on every existing auxiliary, including every retained $K_j$. Every marked/unmarked test below uses the **specified Lüders instrument**
$$\mathcal I_a(Z)=\Pi_aZ\Pi_a,\qquad a\in\{0,1\},$$
in the sense of [[def-qc-instrument-and-conditional-state]]: its positive-probability conditional density is $\mathcal I_a(Z)/\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal I_a(Z))$; no conditional state is assigned when that trace is zero. Execute the test by appending $|0\rangle_F|0\rangle_J$, applying $B_{\mathcal M}$, reading only the fresh flag with the explicitly chosen computational-basis Lüders maps $Y\mapsto Q_aYQ_a$, where $Q_a=I\otimes|a\rangle\langle a|_F\otimes I_J$, storing $a$ in the classical output record, and applying $B_{\mathcal M}^*$ to return the fresh flag and scratch to zero. Retain every pre-existing register; on an unmarked result read no finer first-label information. A marked result may then be followed by label readout and verification for output. Charge one forward check, one inverse check, and one flag readout per test, hence $O(C)$ in the stated query/check profile. The recursive marked phase flip is implemented by $B_{\mathcal M}$, a phase $-1$ on flag $1$, and $B_{\mathcal M}^*$, also with both calls charged.

**Approximate stationary reflection $R(\beta)$.** Set $s=\min\{q\ge1:4^q\delta_0\ge64\}$ and $k=\min\{j\ge1:2^j\beta\ge2\}$, using exact integer/rational comparisons. With $Q=2^s$, these comparisons give $Q\ge8/\sqrt{\delta_0}>2\pi/\sqrt{\delta_0}$ using $\pi<4$ from [[thm-gregory-leibniz-series-for-pi-from-a-finite-remainder]]. Append $k$ separate $s$-bit zero phase registers. Coherently execute the finite QPE circuit prefix from [[alg-qa-quantum-phase-estimation]] on $W$ in each register, using the declared controlled powers. This prefix is a unitary circuit on the full walk register and is executed on arbitrary walk states, including superpositions; the eigenvector input in the QPE analysis is not a restriction on the circuit's action. Do not measure these phase registers. If at least one phase register is nonzero, apply $-I$ to the walk state. If all are zero, apply the exact controlled row-space reflection $R_A=2TT^*-I$ using the charged row-preparation, inverse, and clean-state reflection calls. Reverse the $k$ coherent QPE prefixes in reverse chronological order, using the supplied controlled inverse powers. Charge $2k(2^s-1)$ controlled $W$ and $W^*$ calls, the controlled $R_A$ branch, all-zero comparisons, phase-register gates, and the allocated classical arithmetic. The all-zero branch is required: $W$ has the extra zero-phase subspace $A^\perp\cap B^\perp$, where $R_A=-I$, while $R_A=+I$ on the stationary state.

**Recursive circuit $A_i$.** Let $\gamma=1/120$, $\beta_i=\gamma/(16i^2)$ for $i\ge1$, and $A_0=I$. For $i>0$, allocate a fresh $K_i$ for $R(\beta_i)$ and execute chronologically: (i) $A_{i-1}$, the marked phase flip, and $A_{i-1}^\dagger$; (ii) coherently test every older $K_j$, $j<i$, applying $-I$ if any is nonzero and otherwise applying $R(\beta_i)$ on the walk and fresh $K_i$; compute and uncompute the control predicate; (iii) apply $A_{i-1}$. Each $\beta_i$ is rational, and the $k_i$ loop in $R(\beta_i)$ is an exact rational comparison. An inverse means the exact reversed finite gate list, not a reset of measured work.

**Tolerant finding wrapper.** If $\varepsilon_0\ge1/2$, take $n_s=\min\{n\ge1:2^{-n}\le\rho\}$ fresh stationary samples, verify each label, return the first marked label, and output `NO MARKED` if all fail. Otherwise, let $t_{\max}$ be the least integer $t\ge0$ such that $3^t\arcsin\sqrt{\varepsilon_0}\ge\pi/4$. Determine it by the exact algebraic threshold comparison $\varepsilon_0\ge\sin^2(\pi/(4\cdot3^t))$; equality takes the $\ge$ branch. Let $n_{\rm out}=\min\{n\ge1:(19/20)^n\le\rho\}$, found by exact rational comparisons. In each outer trial:

1. Prepare a fresh stationary sample, test its first label, and return it if marked.
2. Prepare a fresh stationary walk state with all $K_1,\ldots,K_{t_{\max}}$ zero.
3. For $i=1,\ldots,t_{\max}$, apply $A_i$, execute the marked/unmarked Lüders test specified above, and on a marked outcome read, verify, and return the label. On an unmarked outcome retain the conditional current state and all auxiliary registers, and continue; do not reprepare or reset them.
4. If no level succeeds, discard the trial and begin the next fresh outer trial.

If all trials fail, output `NO MARKED`. Every loop has a finite cap; all confidence calculations, comparisons, reversible predicates, retained auxiliary space, state preparation, update, inverse, controlled, reflection, and check costs are charged. In the $\varepsilon_0\ge1/2$ branch, the cap above gives false-negative probability at most $\rho$; in the other branch correctness and the sharper cost are proved separately in [[thm-qa-18-reversible-search-cost]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, let $K$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite instrument** from $H$ to $K$ is a family of complex-linear maps $\mathcal I_a:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$, one for each $a\in\Omega$, such that each $\mathcal I_a$ is completely positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and

$$\sum_{a\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative with trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), define the outcome weight $p_a(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(\rho))$. The **conditional state** for outcome $a$ is

$$\rho_a:=\begin{cases}\mathcal I_a(\rho)/p_a(\rho),&p_a(\rho)>0,\\[2pt]\bot,&p_a(\rho)=0.\end{cases}$$

Here $\bot$ is a symbol meaning that no conditional density operator is assigned; it is not a state. Positivity and normalization of the outcome weights, and density of every positive-probability conditional state, are proved in [[thm-qc-instrument-outcome-law-normalizes]] and [[thm-qc-instrument-conditional-state-is-density]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $V$ be a normed space. For all $x,y\in V$,
$$\bigl|\|x\|-\|y\|\bigr|\le \|x-y\|.$$
In particular, the norm map is $1$-Lipschitz for the norm metric.

For every finite row-stochastic kernel, the map $T$ of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]] satisfies $T^*T=I$ and is an isometry, and the matrix entries of $D=T^*ST$ are

$$D_{xy}=\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}.$$

Hence $D$ is real symmetric, self-adjoint, and $\|D\|\le1$. If $(X,P,\pi)$ is also finite reversible, then

$$D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt\pi)\,P\,\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt\pi).$$

Every eigenvalue of $D$ is real and belongs to $[-1,1]$. The empty state set has the zero endomorphism and empty spectrum; the similarity assertion is only made when a positive stationary probability vector is supplied.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite POVM on $H$, and let $M_a=E_a^{1/2}$ be the nonnegative square root of each effect. The maps

$$\mathcal I_a(X):=M_aXM_a,\qquad X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

form an instrument from $H$ to itself.

Let $\rho$ be a density operator and $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ a finite projective measurement on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$. Put $p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$. If $p_a>0$, then

$$\rho_a:=\frac{P_a\rho P_a}{p_a}$$

is a density operator whose image $\operatorname{im}(\rho_a):=\{\rho_a x:x\in H\}$ is contained in $\operatorname{im}(P_a)$ ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]). This statement assigns a conditional state only on positive-probability branches.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the stationary eigenvalue $1$ is simple and every other eigenvalue of the reversible transition operator has $|\lambda|\le1-\delta_{\rm act}\le1-\delta_0$. By [F20], the discriminant is similar to this transition operator and has the same eigenvalues; the stationary eigenvector corresponds to $\sqrt\pi$. In the two-reflection Szegedy walk, the circular phase distance of a nonstationary signal eigenvalue is $d_{\mathbb T}(\arccos(\lambda)/\pi)=\arccos(|\lambda|)/\pi$. For $t=\arccos(1-\delta_0)\in[0,\pi/2]$, [F14] and [F15] give $\delta_0=1-\cos t=2\sin^2(t/2)\le t^2/2$, so $t\ge\sqrt{2\delta_0}$. Thus every nonstationary signal phase has circular distance at least $\sqrt{2\delta_0}/\pi$. The only additional zero-phase subspace is the walk-space orthogonal complement in [F3], on which the exact row-space reflection $R_A$ equals $-I$; on the stationary vector it equals $+I$.

In $R(\beta)$, the QPE scale satisfies $Q=2^s\ge8/\sqrt{\delta_0}>2\pi/\sqrt{\delta_0}$ by the algorithm's exact integer test and $\pi<4$ from [F11]. On the stationary phase $0$, [F7] returns outcome $0$ in every register, so the all-zero branch applies $R_A=+I$ and uncomputes; the stationary state is fixed exactly. For a nonzero signal phase at circular distance $d\ge\sqrt{\delta_0}/\pi$, the outcome-kernel [F5] and the geometric sum [F6] give $\Pr(y=0)\le\frac{1}{4Q^2d^2}<\frac1{16}$. The first inequality follows because $|1-\exp(2\pi i\theta)|=2\sin(\pi d)\ge4d$ and $|1-\exp(2\pi iQ\theta)|\le2$. Repeating QPE coherently in $k=\min\{j\ge1:2^j\beta\ge2\}$ fresh phase registers makes the all-zero branch norm at most $4^{-k}$. On a nonzero signal eigenvector, the actual reflection differs from the ideal $-I$ only on that branch, where it applies $R_A$; before QPE uncomputation the difference is $(R_A+I)$ on the all-zero component. By [F20], $R_A=2\Pi_A-I$ for the orthogonal projection $\Pi_A=TT^*$, so $R_A+I=2\Pi_A$ and orthogonal decomposition gives $\|\Pi_Aw\|\le\|w\|$; hence the coherent state error is at most $2\cdot4^{-k}\le2^{1-k}\le\beta$. Reversing the QPE prefixes is unitary and preserves this norm bound. For each nonzero eigenphase, the $k$ QPE circuits use fresh registers and leave the walker eigenvector unchanged, so the joint all-zero probability is the product of the single-register bounds and is at most $16^{-k}$. For a superposition of eigenspaces, the joint all-zero branch is still block-diagonal in the orthogonal eigenspaces; expanding its squared norm gives the eigenspace-weighted average of these joint probabilities (the same orthogonal calculation as [F8]). Its branch norm is therefore at most $4^{-k}$ times the input norm, and the same estimate applies. On $A^\perp\cap B^\perp$, the phase is exactly zero and $R_A=-I$, so the algorithm also agrees exactly with the ideal reflection there. Thus the bound is a coherent state-vector bound, not just an outcome-probability statement.

The projectors $\Pi_0,\Pi_1$ of the algorithm are self-adjoint idempotents summing to identity. For each $a$, $\langle\Pi_av,v\rangle=\|\Pi_av\|^2\ge0$, so they form a POVM by [F21]; each $\Pi_a$ is its own nonnegative square root. The square-root-instrument theorem in [F21] therefore proves that the selected maps $Z\mapsto\Pi_aZ\Pi_a$ are a finite instrument, and its projective conditional-state theorem applies on positive-probability branches. For a unit vector $\psi$ of the whole existing register space, the algorithm's clean check sends $\psi|0\rangle_F|0\rangle_J$ to $\sum_{a=0}^1(\Pi_a\psi)|a\rangle_F|0\rangle_J$. The specified computational Lüders readout of the fresh flag selects precisely $(\Pi_a\psi)|a\rangle_F|0\rangle_J$; after recording $a$, the inverse check maps this vector to $(\Pi_a\psi)|0\rangle_F|0\rangle_J$. The resulting branch on the original registers is thus exactly $\Pi_a|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\Pi_a=|\Pi_a\psi\rangle\langle\Pi_a\psi|$. Its coordinate trace is $\sum_j|(\Pi_a\psi)_j|^2=\|\Pi_a\psi\|^2=p_a$ by [F16] and [F21]. If $p_a>0$, division gives the pure conditional vector $\Pi_a\psi/\|\Pi_a\psi\|$; if $p_a=0$, the branch has zero weight and no conditional state. The identities hold on all retained auxiliary registers, even when entangled with the first label; only the fresh flag and scratch are cleared. Each test uses one forward check, one inverse check and one separately priced flag readout, so it costs $O(C)$ in the algorithm's query/check profile. The same compute/phase/uncompute word implements the exact marked phase flip with two check calls and its separately priced phase gate.

Let $\Pi$ be any orthogonal projection and let $\xi,\zeta$ be unit vectors with $\|\xi-\zeta\|\le\Delta$. Put $a=\Pi\xi$ and $b=\Pi\zeta$. By [F16], $\Pi$ is contractive, so $\|a-b\|\le\Delta$; [F19] gives $|\|a\|-\|b\||\le\Delta$. If $\|b\|\ge2/3$ and the actual projected branch has positive probability (so $\|a\|>0$), [F18] yields $$\left\|\frac a{\|a\|}-\frac b{\|b\|}\right\|\le\frac{\|a-b\|+|\|a\|-\|b\||}{\|b\|}\le3\Delta.$$ The same estimate applies when one input is an ideal state and the other differs by a known reflection-error vector.

For the recursive branch suppose $0<p:=\pi(\mathcal M)<1/2$ and put $\phi_0=\arcsin\sqrt p$. If $p\ge1/2$, the initial stationary sample already succeeds with probability at least $1/2$, by [F1] and [F16], so no angle analysis is needed. In an exact recursive amplitude-amplification step, the marked phase flip followed by reflection about the current state triples its marked angle. In the ordered marked/unmarked basis, write $s=\sin\phi,c=\cos\phi$ and $|\psi\rangle=(s,c)$. The reflection matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2s^2-1&2sc\\2sc&2c^2-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-\cos2\phi&\sin2\phi\\\sin2\phi&\cos2\phi\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplying it by $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)(s,c)=(-s,c)$ gives first coordinate $s\cos2\phi+c\sin2\phi=3s-4s^3=\sin3\phi$ and second coordinate $-s\sin2\phi+c\cos2\phi=4c^3-3c=\cos3\phi$, using [F13] and [F14]. At level $i$, let $\phi_i$ be the actual angle after $A_i$, let $\bar\phi_i=3^i\phi_0$, and put $e_i=|\sin\phi_i-\sin\bar\phi_i|$. Let $t$ be the first ideal index with $\bar\phi_t\ge\pi/4$; then $\bar\phi_t<3\pi/4$ and, if $t\ge2$, every $i\le t-1$ has $\bar\phi_{i-1}<\pi/12$. Inductively $e_{i-1}\le\gamma\bar\phi_{i-1}/\pi$ implies $\sin\phi_{i-1}\le\sin(\pi/12)+\gamma/12$. By [F11] and [F15], the right side is less than $7/24+1/1440<1/2$, while $\sin(\pi/4)>1/2$ by [F17]; hence both angles lie in $[0,\pi/4]$. On the input to the level-$i$ approximate stationary reflection, after conjugating by $A_{i-1}^\dagger$, the component orthogonal to the stationary vector has norm $|\sin(2\phi_{i-1})|$. By step 1.2 the reflection error on that component has norm at most $\beta_i|\sin(2\phi_{i-1})|$. The marked-amplitude change is no larger than this norm: the marked projector is orthogonal by [F16], so its orthogonal decomposition makes it contractive, and [F19] bounds the change in projected norms by the vector error. To compare triple angles, set $x=\sin a,y=\sin b$ for $a,b\in[0,\pi/4]$, so $x,y\in[0,1/\sqrt2]$ by [F14]. The identity $\sin2a=2x\sqrt{1-x^2}$ shows that the absolute difference of the two double-angle values is at most $2|x-y|$: for $x\ge y$, the function $2x\sqrt{1-x^2}$ is increasing because its square difference is $4(x^2-y^2)(1-x^2-y^2)\ge0$, while $2x\sqrt{1-x^2}-2y\sqrt{1-y^2}=2(x-y)\sqrt{1-x^2}+2y\bigl(\sqrt{1-x^2}-\sqrt{1-y^2}\bigr)\le2(x-y).$ The case $y\ge x$ is symmetric. By [F13], the triple-angle difference is $(x-y)(3-4(x^2+xy+y^2))$, whose coefficient has absolute value at most $3$ because $0\le x^2+xy+y^2\le3/2$. Therefore, for $i\le t-1$, $e_i\le\beta_i\bigl(\sin(2\bar\phi_{i-1})+2e_{i-1}\bigr)+3e_{i-1}\le 2\beta_i(\bar\phi_{i-1}+e_{i-1})+3e_{i-1}.$ For these indices $\sin(2\bar\phi_{i-1})\le2\bar\phi_{i-1}$ by [F15], so the last inequality follows.

Define $\tilde e_0=0$ and $\tilde e_i=4\beta_i\bar\phi_{i-1}+3\tilde e_{i-1}$. Suppose inductively that $e_{i-1}\le\tilde e_{i-1}\le\bar\phi_{i-1}$; then step 2.1 gives $e_i\le\tilde e_i$. For $N\ge4$ and $2\le r\le\lfloor N/2\rfloor$, the **lazy Johnson walk** has state space $\Omega_r=\{S\subseteq[N]:|S|=r\}$ and transitions

$$P(S,S)=\tfrac12,\qquad P(S,S\setminus\{i\}\cup\{j\})=\frac{1}{2r(N-r)}\quad(i\in S,\ j\notin S),$$

with all other entries zero. Its marked vertices are

$$\mathcal M_f:=\{S\in\Omega_r:\exists i,j\in S,\ i\ne j,\ f(i)=f(j)\}.$$

The stored data at $S$ are the $r$ labeled values $(f(i))_{i\in S}$. Preparing the uniform $r$-subset state and loading these values has value-query cost $S_0=r$, with subset preparation gates charged separately. A neighbor update erases the removed value and loads the added value, so its value-query cost is $U_0=2$; the XOR oracle is its own inverse. Checking whether the stored subset is marked uses no further value queries, so $C_0=0$, but comparison gates and memory accesses are charged. Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For a linear subspace $W$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) of an inner product space $V$, using the preceding notion of orthogonality ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]), its **orthogonal complement** is

$$W^\perp:=\{v\in V:\langle v,w\rangle=0\text{ for every }w\in W\}.$$

This is a linear subspace: $0\in W^\perp$, and linearity in the first argument shows that $au+bv\in W^\perp$ whenever $u,v\in W^\perp$ and $a,b$ are scalars. One has $V^\perp=\{0\}$ by positive definiteness and $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

A **finite reversible Markov chain** is a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$ together with a supplied probability vector $\pi=(\pi_x)_{x\in X}$ such that $\pi_x>0$ for every $x$, $\sum_x\pi_x=1$, $\pi P=\pi$, and

$$\pi_xP_{xy}=\pi_yP_{yx}\qquad(x,y\in X).$$

The stationary law and detailed balance are explicit input hypotheses; the definition does not invoke a theorem that produces a stationary law. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is assumed. In particular, a periodic reversible chain is included.

For a finite reversible chain $(X,P,\pi)$, let $H_0=\{f:\sum_x\pi_xf_x=0\}$ with the weighted inner product from [[lem-qa-17-reversible-transition-self-adjoint-on-l2-pi]]. Define its **absolute spectral gap** by

$$\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P):=1-\|P|_{H_0}\|_{2,\pi}.$$

The norm of the restriction to the zero subspace is $0$ by [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]], so a one-state chain has absolute gap $1$. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is built into this definition: a reducible chain with a nonconstant stationary vector in $H_0$ can have gap $0$, and a periodic chain can have gap $0$ because of an eigenvalue $-1$. The eigenvalue form of the definition is proved in [[thm-qa-17-absolute-gap-eigenvalue-characterization]].

Expanding the finite sums with this convention gives $$ \langle R_k f,g\rangle=\sum_A f(A)\,\overline{\sum_{b\notin A}g(A\cup\{b\})}=\langle f,L_{k+1}g\rangle; $$ by [F4], $L_{k+1}=R_k^*$. Put $L_0:V_0\to\{0\}$ equal to zero. For $0\le k<r$ and $f\in V_k$, the diagonal terms in $L_{k+1}R_k f$ occur $N-k$ times, the diagonal terms in $R_{k-1}L_kf$ occur $k$ times, and both have the same off-diagonal replacement terms. Hence $L_{k+1}R_k-R_{k-1}L_k=(N-2k)I_{V_k}$, where the second term is zero for $k=0$.

Taking the inner product of the identity in step 1.1 with $f$ gives $\|R_kf\|^2=\|L_kf\|^2+(N-2k)\|f\|^2$. Since $k<N/2$ for $0\le k<r$, $R_k$ is injective, so [F2] gives $\dim\operatorname{ran}R_k=\dim V_k$. By [F4] and [F5], $\ker L_{k+1}=\ker R_k^*=(\operatorname{ran}R_k)^\perp$. Applying [F2] to $L_{k+1}$ then yields $\dim\operatorname{ran}L_{k+1}=\dim V_k$, so $L_{k+1}:V_{k+1}\to V_k$ is onto. Put $H_0=V_0$ and $H_j=\ker L_j$ for $1\le j\le r$; [F2] gives $\dim H_j=\binom Nj-\binom N{j-1}$.

Empty products of raising maps mean the identity. If it holds at $t$ and $j+t<r$, apply the commutator at level $j+t$; the coefficient becomes $t(N-2j-t+1)+(N-2j-2t)=(t+1)(N-2j-t)$, proving the formula for $t+1$.

On $V_r$, the Johnson adjacency operator is $A=R_{r-1}L_r-rI$: the $r$ diagonal choices in $R_{r-1}L_r$ return the same subset, and every other term replaces exactly one element. Since $L_r=R_{r-1}^*$ by step 1.1, [F6] gives $A^*=A$. For $j<r$, applying step 3.1 with $t=r-j$ shows that $R_{r-1}\cdots R_jH_j$ is an eigenspace of $A$ with eigenvalue $(r-j)(N-r-j+1)-r$. For $j=r$, the empty raising product is the identity on $H_r$, and $L_rH_r=0$ gives $A|_{H_r}=-rI$ directly, the same formula. The raising maps are injective by step 2.1, so this eigenspace has dimension $\dim H_j$. These eigenvalues are distinct because consecutive values differ by $N-2j>0$ for $j<r\le N/2$. For $v,w$ in eigenspaces with distinct eigenvalues $\alpha,\beta$, self-adjointness gives $(\alpha-\beta)\langle v,w\rangle=\langle Av,w\rangle-\langle v,Aw\rangle=0$; hence the eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal. Their dimensions sum telescopically to $\binom Nr=\dim V_r$, so their direct sum is all of $V_r$.

The nonlazy transition is $A/[r(N-r)]$ by [F1], and the lazy transition is its average with the identity. Therefore its eigenvalue on the $j$th eigenspace is $\frac12\left(1+\frac{(r-j)(N-r-j+1)-r}{r(N-r)}\right)=1-\frac{j(N+1-j)}{2r(N-r)}.$ The transitions are symmetric and row-stochastic, so the uniform positive law is stationary and satisfies detailed balance; [F7] makes this a finite reversible chain and defines its absolute gap on the mean-zero subspace. The $j=0$ eigenspace has multiplicity one and is spanned by the constant vector. The number containing a fixed pair $\{a,b\}$ is $\binom{N-2}{r-2}$, so its uniform probability is $\frac{\binom{N-2}{r-2}}{\binom Nr}=\frac{r(r-1)}{N(N-1)}.$ Every subset containing this colliding pair is marked, so the marked stationary mass is at least this value.

Apply [F1] to the lazy walk in [F2]. Its stationary law is uniform and its absolute gap is the displayed $\delta$; the nonnegative spectrum rules out a negative-eigenvalue obstruction to the absolute gap. For any positive rational $q\le1$, let $\operatorname{dyad}(q)=2^{-j}$ for the least integer $j\ge0$ with $2^{-j}\le q$; exact rational comparisons compute it and give $q/2\le\operatorname{dyad}(q)\le q$. Supply the dyadic lower gap bound $\delta_0=\operatorname{dyad}(\delta)$. The initial stored list requires one query for each of its $r$ values. Replacing one selected index by one unselected index erases the old stored value with one inverse value query and loads the new value with one forward value query. The marked check compares the already stored values, so it costs no additional value query. Explicitly, the basis permutation $|S,d,b\rangle\mapsto|S,d,b\mathbin\oplus c(d)\rangle$, where $c(d)$ is the collision bit of the stored list, is a clean coherent check: it preserves the list, needs no value-oracle call, and is its own inverse. Tensoring identity on every other existing register gives exactly the check interface in [F3]; its fresh-flag Lüders readout and inverse therefore add zero value queries as well, with gates and readout resources separate. These are stored-vertex setup and elementary replacement costs. The coherent row construction [F4] separately supplies the stronger access inputs required by [F3], with stationary edge setup $S_0\le r+2$, common controlled-walk/inverse/row-reflection bound $U_0=8$, and $C=0$.

Put $\varepsilon_*=r(r-1)/[N(N-1)]$ and supply the dyadic lower marked-mass bound $\varepsilon_0=\operatorname{dyad}(\varepsilon_*)$. For $r\ge2$ and $N\ge4$, $r-1\ge r/2$ and $N(N-1)\le N^2$, hence $\varepsilon_*\ge r^2/(2N^2)$ and $\varepsilon_0\ge\varepsilon_*/2\ge r^2/(4N^2)$. Also $r\le N/2$ gives $\delta=N/[2r(N-r)]\ge1/(2r)$, so $\delta_0\ge\delta/2\ge1/(4r)$ by step 2.1. Since $r\le N/2$, $\varepsilon_*\le(N-2)/(4(N-1))<1/2$, so [F3] applies even if the actual marked mass is larger. Run the wrapper with the dyadic failure target $\rho=1/2$. By [F3] and [F4], its query bound is $r+2+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0}}\frac{8}{\sqrt{\delta_0}}\right)\le r+O\!\left(\frac Nr\sqrt r\right)=r+O(N/\sqrt r)$, with the additive $2$ absorbed since $N/\sqrt r\ge1$. The measured set is marked; by [F2] it contains two indices with equal stored values, and scanning those $r$ stored values identifies such a pair without a new value-oracle query.

For $N\ge8$, $N^{2/3}\le N/2$; for $4\le N\le7$, the displayed clamp selects an admissible integer in $[2,\lfloor N/2\rfloor]$. The clamp differs from $N^{2/3}$ by only fixed factors over this finite range and is $\Theta(N^{2/3})$ for all $N\ge4$. Therefore both $r$ and $N/\sqrt r$ are $O(N^{2/3})$. If $N\le3$, the definition specifies direct pairwise value comparison instead of a Johnson walk; querying each value once uses at most $N$ value queries.
